metadata.name: Robust Research Task
metadata.description: Исследовательский вариант robust-task: планирование, исполнение каждого шага и все гейты выполняются субагентами, которые ОБЯЗАНЫ сначала прочитать весь корпус исследования ЦЕЛИКОМ и судить как пир по существу (чтением+рассуждением, а не grep/подсчётом). Замороженный-но-расширяемый corpus-manifest, retry/эскалация, Telegram, восстановление контекста. Процесс: UNDERSTAND → BUILD-CORPUS → PLAN(subagent) → VALIDATE → APPROVE → (EXECUTE(subagent) → GATE)×N → VERIFY → FINAL-REVIEW → DELIVER.

nodes.directive:
Gather a real, deep understanding of the task and its GOAL from the user — this is a conversation to understand, NOT a form to fill.

Establish, by talking with the user (ask what you genuinely need, in your own words):
1. What needs to be done and WHY — the real end goal for its consumer/reader.
2. What an EXCELLENT result looks like for that consumer, and what DEPTH is required (depth over breadth).
3. The GOAL'S FACETS — the distinct things the result must deliver (derive them for THIS task, whatever it is: e.g. correctness, understandability, coherent narrative, navigation, a working artifact…).
4. Constraints (time, resources, dependencies).
5. How we will know it is genuinely done — success criteria that cover the GOAL (including the usefulness/quality/depth axis when the task is research/writing/design/etc.), not only mechanical correctness. Criteria MAY be qualitative when that is what matters — for each such criterion, state HOW it will be judged (by reading against a rubric).
6. The RESEARCH SCOPE — which sources / files / areas / codebases the result must be grounded in. This feeds the next step (setup-corpus), which enumerates the full corpus every subagent will be required to read in full. Capture it broadly: name the artifacts, docs, code, prior research and data that ground this task.

Do NOT transcribe these fields back at the user mechanically. Understand first. The task may be ANYTHING (code, research, architecture design, an essay, a 3D model, data analysis, …) — use judgement; do not force it into a template.

Planning standards (context for what a good plan and good criteria need):
{{planning_standards}}

Fold the goal, its FACETS, and the required DEPTH into expected_deliverable and success_criteria (there is no separate facet field — capture them there in words; the plan will trace items to these facets).

⚠️ MANDATORY: WAIT FOR USER RESPONSE
- Ask questions and STOP
- DO NOT fill fields until the user explicitly responds
- Record in user_response_text exactly what the user wrote

⚠️ AFTER RECEIVING RESPONSE:
- Formulate a short task name (2-5 words) for task_short_name
- This name will be used for progress tracking
nodes.completionCondition: User EXPLICITLY answered questions (response text exists in user_response_text)

nodes.directive:
Build the execution plan by DELEGATING to a PLANNER SUBAGENT (a teammate). Do NOT plan inline yourself. Spawn one subagent with the brief below and record its result.

[DELEGATION — SPELL OUT THE FULL-READ IMPERATIVE TO THE SUBAGENT]
When you spawn the subagent, do NOT hand off silently and do NOT assume it will read the brief carefully. In YOUR OWN words, tell it directly: (1) WHY it must read ALL project/corpus files IN FULL here — the reasoning is entangled across files, so a partial read misses the cross-dependencies and produces wrong conclusions; (2) that a full read is NEAR-MANDATORY, not optional — this holds for planning, for doing the work, and for EVERY validation; (3) exactly WHAT to read: the whole corpus in {{corpus_manifest_path}} plus this step's specific artifacts. Subagents routinely UNDER-read to save tokens — counter that head-on: make explicit that skimming to save tokens is unacceptable and that its judgment is worthless if it did not actually read everything. Pass this as a direct instruction, not merely the pasted brief.

DELEGATION — DO NOT CAGE THE SUBAGENT: the subagent is the SAME model as you, with the same judgment. Hand it the GOAL, the full CONTEXT, and the peer principle below — then TRUST it to decide what to read closely, what matters, and how to assess. Do NOT over-narrow it ("read exactly these", rigid output formats, coordinate grids, step-by-step scripts). Over-narrowing mutes the very judgment you spawned it for; a subagent does better when it gets a goal and freedom, not a cage.

[YOU ARE A PEER — READ THE WHOLE THING, THEN JUDGE ON THE MERITS]
You are a senior researcher/architect on this task — the SAME capability as whoever handed it to
you, with the same judgment. You were given the material and the goal; your job is to understand
it deeply and reason about it, not to fill a form, follow a checklist, or stamp coordinates.

READ THE ENTIRE RESEARCH CONTENT IN FULL before you conclude anything (the sources are enumerated
in {{corpus_manifest_path}} — that list tells you WHAT the whole is; task-requirements.md is the
frozen goal). This is not bureaucracy — it is the only way to do this right, and here is WHY, concretely:
- In real research the parts are not independent: a conclusion in one place almost always RESTS ON
  or is ENTANGLED WITH reasoning, evidence, or decisions made ELSEWHERE. Those links are usually
  NOT visible from the structure — what a section depends on is rarely the section next to it — and
  they are NOT findable by grep/search, because the connection is conceptual (a shared assumption,
  a chain of inference, a hidden contradiction), not a keyword.
- What that failure looks like:
   · A headline conclusion — "no existing engine fits our needs" — actually rests entirely on ONE
     library's analysis buried in another chapter. Read only the conclusion and you'd never see it's
     over-broad; the fix depends on a part you'd never grep for.
   · An architecture decision silently contradicts a requirement stated three files earlier. Neither
     keyword surfaces the clash — only having read BOTH, and holding them together, reveals it.
   · A whole later branch of the research is built on an early inference that, read closely, doesn't
     hold — so everything downstream is load-bearing on sand.
- If you skim, or read only the "relevant-looking" parts, or navigate by grep, you will MISS exactly
  these cross-dependencies — and that is precisely where the real problems (and the real insights)
  live. Word-search finds strings; it cannot tell you whether an argument holds across the whole.

So read all of it, holding the connections in your head. grep/search/counting are fine as a
NAVIGATION aid or to check a purely mechanical fact (does this link resolve, does this build) —
never as a substitute for reading, and never as how you judge whether something is sound. If you
find an in-scope source not in the manifest, add it and read it too; growing scope is fine, silently
narrowing it is not.

Then reason like a senior reviewer told "tear this apart on the merits": where does the logical
chain break and why; where do conclusions hang in the air (including about libraries); where does
the structure go in circles; are there real architectural alternatives and how do they compare; is
it honest about depth and examples. Point to a specific place IN WORDS when it genuinely helps
("the 'no engine fits' conclusion holds only for Rive") — not because you owe coordinates everywhere.

JUDGMENT IS NOT A COORDINATE. For factual/technical claims (code runs, a test passes, a link
resolves, a quoted fact is accurate, a path exists) the right evidence is a tool result / file:line.
For JUDGMENT claims (is the logic sound, does the chain hold, is the structure coherent, are the
conclusions warranted, is the architecture good, is it clear and deep) the "evidence" IS your
reasoned argument in prose — a line number, a coverage grid, a proof-of-read ledger is a category
error: it is an ADDRESS, not an assessment. Do not produce one; do not demand one.

You do NOT produce a per-file ledger, a coverage grid, or a proof-of-read. Your assessment itself
must reflect the WHOLE — a real senior judgment cannot be faked from a skim, and a peer who also
read everything will notice if it was.

PLANNER BRIEF (verbatim):
  After you have fully read the corpus, build a plan that LEADS TO THE GOAL (not to "mechanical checks pass"). Start from the end goal + real consumer, derive the goal's FACETS and required DEPTH, THEN decompose. Carry a one-paragraph ARGUMENT: why this structure reaches the goal, grounded in what you actually read.
  Frame each item as a GOAL + the CRITERIA for a good result — trust the executing peer to decide HOW — and give each item its Execution: DELEGATE|INLINE marker per the planning standards.
  Each step: one action, states which GOAL FACET it serves, and carries ITS OWN GATE (a substance/quality criterion judged by READING; a technical floor only where a genuinely machine-checkable part exists — necessary, not sufficient). Every facet covered by ≥1 step.
  Anchor steps on RESULTS/questions, not pre-carved artifacts; mark provisional items PROVISIONAL.
  OUTCOME-DEPENDENCY CHECK: judge whether later steps genuinely depend on the RESULTS of earlier ones (a reasoned chain where fixing an early link cascades downstream). If so, do NOT fabricate a detailed full plan — plan the near horizon concretely, mark the rest PROVISIONAL, and put an explicit re-planning/decision point, using approach A (child-flow-with-inherited-context) or B (planned recursive teleport-replan) from the planning standards. Trying to pre-plan work whose shape depends on results you don't have yet is the mistake, not thoroughness.
  Follow the planning standards: {{planning_standards}}

  Into EACH plan item, WRITE its [PLAN-ITEM INVARIANTS] (both in plan.md and in the steps[].action text) so an isolated executor cannot lose them:
  [PLAN-ITEM INVARIANTS]
  Every plan item embeds, inside the item text, the research invariants it must not violate (violating ANY = the item is failed even if everything else is perfect):
   read the whole corpus first; produce explanatory narrative not tags; give WHAT/WHY/HOW per mechanism; cross-link every reference; no process meta-marks; hit the required depth. The item also restates the specific goal/requirements it serves (so an isolated executor keeps them).

  Save the plan to {{workspace_path}}/plan.md (one numbered item per step: Why / What to do / Serves facet / Expected output / GATE / embedded PLAN-ITEM INVARIANTS).

  The plan and every item must aim the eventual OUTPUT at this bar:
  [OUTPUT QUALITY RUBRIC]
  The OUTPUT (not just the reading) must meet this bar wherever the task is research/writing/explanatory:
   - EXPLANATORY PROSE, not a telegraphic term-stream: connected narrative with intro and conclusion; code/data woven into the flow, not dumped as labelled blocks.
   - Every mechanism/term gives WHAT (plain-words essence before first use) → WHY (the problem it solves; what a naive approach would do) → HOW (enough for the reader to get the idea), and ONLY THEN a reference as deepening — never a bare "see X.Y" IN PLACE of understanding.
   - CROSS-LINK every reference to its definition+example where the medium allows.
   - NO process meta-marks in the deliverable ("review done", "for engineer", "step N trace").
   - REWRITE telegraphic passages into explanatory ones — do NOT merely gloss/annotate on top.
   - Real DEPTH over breadth; no name-drop passing as coverage.

Return total_steps and plan_saved_to_file.
nodes.completionCondition: Plan built by a subagent that first read the whole corpus; plan saved to plan.md

nodes.directive:
Show user the task execution plan.

Task: {{understand-task.task_description}}
Expected result: {{understand-task.expected_deliverable}}

Present the plan from {{workspace_path}}/plan.md ({{total_steps}} steps). Note the research corpus size: {{corpus_file_count}} sources enumerated in the corpus manifest (every subagent must read them all in full).

Success will be measured by criteria:
{{understand-task.success_criteria}}

⚠️ MANDATORY: WAIT FOR USER RESPONSE
- Ask: 'Do you confirm the plan? (yes/no)'
- STOP and wait until the user writes a response
- DO NOT fill plan_approved until the user explicitly says yes or no
- Showing the plan ≠ getting confirmation
- Record in user_response_text exactly what the user answered

⚠️ HANDLING FEEDBACK:
- Any comment, suggested change, or anything other than a pure 'yes' → plan_approved: 'no'
- Record comments in revision_feedback
- 'Yes, but...' = NO; 'Good, just change...' = NO
- Only a pure 'yes'/'ok'/'confirm' without reservations = YES

DO NOT fix the plan yourself. Reply plan_approved = 'no' with revision_feedback — the workflow routes to the fix branch.

If the user does NOT approve, do NOT use teleport-replan and do NOT fix the plan yourself — just answer plan_approved='no' with revision_feedback; the workflow routes to the revise-plan branch. teleport-replan is ONLY for mid-execution replans, not plan rejection.
nodes.completionCondition: User EXPLICITLY answered yes or no (response text exists in user_response_text)

nodes.directive:
Revise plan based on user comments.

- Keep the original FROZEN requirements and goal facets — do not lose them.
- PRESERVE the corpus manifest ({{corpus_manifest_path}}): the corpus may GROW (append newly in-scope sources) but must NOT silently shrink.
- Carry forward every plan item that is STILL RELEVANT — do not drop still-valid work.
- Do NOT silently narrow scope: if the revision reduces scope or removes content, EXPLICITLY name what would be lost and get the user's OK first. Read the current plan file in FULL before overwriting it.

Read the current plan from {{workspace_path}}/plan.md IN FULL, revise it per the feedback (preserving the above), and update {{workspace_path}}/plan.md.

EXECUTION VALIDATION CRITERIA:

0. TWO LAYERS — FLOOR vs SUBSTANCE (do not confuse them):
- TECHNICAL FLOOR = the machine-checkable part (build passes, tests pass, links resolve, paths real, no hallucination). A technical floor applies ONLY where a genuinely machine-checkable part exists; where it does, it is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT — "the floor passed" is NEVER the same as "done". MANY research/reasoning items have NO machine-checkable part — do not invent one.
- SUBSTANCE / QUALITY = does the result actually meet the goal for its consumer (clear, deep enough, coherent, fit-for-purpose). Judged by the method that fits: READING against the item's rubric and judgement, not by grep/counting.
- Verify BOTH where both exist. A green floor with unmet substance is NOT done.

1. EVIDENCE IS MANDATORY:
- Each step must have proof of completion appropriate to its gate.
- Evidence types: command output / test result / file / a concrete, specific description; for quality, the reviewer's READING verdict against the rubric.
- 'Done' without details = NOT accepted.

2. STEP VERIFICATION (against the ITEM'S OWN GATE, not a generic checklist):
- Does the result meet the item's gate — both its technical floor and its substance/quality criterion?
- Verify against the PRIMARY SOURCE (the real artifact / code / goal), not the executor's paraphrase.
- Is evidence provided and specific? Are there missing elements? 80% is NOT verified.
- Any defect is treated as a CLASS: find and fix all instances of that pattern across the whole artifact, not just the one spot.

3. TASK VERIFICATION:
- All steps completed (done or explicitly skipped with reason)?
- Every success criterion AND every goal facet actually met by the real deliverable (both directions of traceability)?
- Deliverable ready and fit for the goal, not merely passing mechanical checks?

4. READING DISCIPLINE (this is a research flow — non-dodgeable):
- Every subagent (planner, executor, reviewer) is a PEER and must have read the WHOLE corpus in full first. The subagent's assessment/output must reflect the WHOLE; skim-based work shows and is rejected; the guarantee is judgment + peer review, not a ledger.
- A PARTIAL corpus read = NOT verified.
- Judge quality by READING against the rubric, NOT by grep / counting / keyword-matching. Mechanical tools only for a pure technical floor (link resolves, build/test passes), and only after the full read.

5. OUTPUT SUBSTANCE BAR:
[OUTPUT QUALITY RUBRIC]: EXPLANATORY PROSE not a telegraphic term-stream (intro + flow + conclusion; code/data woven in, not dumped); every mechanism gives WHAT -> WHY -> HOW before any bare reference; cross-link every reference to its definition+example; NO process meta-marks in the deliverable; REWRITE telegraphic passages rather than gloss on top; real DEPTH over breadth (no name-drop as coverage).
[PLAN-ITEM INVARIANTS]: each plan item must carry, in its own text, its research invariants (whole-corpus read first; narrative not tags; WHAT/WHY/HOW; cross-links; no meta-marks; required depth; restated goal/requirements). A missing invariant fails the item.
[REVIEWER CALIBRATION]: reviewers are calibrated to FIND defects; a GREEN verdict is the exception, earned only after a full novice read finds nothing wrong; do NOT default to PASS.

6. NAMED RESEARCH RULES:
R-0 (FINDING = CLASS): any defect is a CLASS — verify/fix it everywhere the pattern occurs, not just the flagged spot.
R-1 (QUALITY BY READING): quality is judged by reading; scripts/grep/counting only for a pure technical floor, never as a quality proxy.

7. JUDGMENT IS NOT A COORDINATE:
- For factual/technical claims (code runs, a test passes, a link resolves, a path exists) the evidence is a tool result / file:line. For JUDGMENT claims (is the logic sound, the structure coherent, the conclusions warranted, the writing clear and deep) the evidence IS the reasoned argument in prose — a line number, a coverage grid, a proof-of-read is a category error (an ADDRESS, not an assessment). Do not produce one; do not demand one.
- VALIDATORS ARE PEERS who judge on the merits by reading + reasoning — never by mechanical conformance to a coordinate grid. A green verdict is an earned reasoned judgment.

TASK DECOMPOSITION PLANNING STANDARDS (single canon):

0. UNIVERSALITY & JUDGEMENT (read first):
- This flow is UNIVERSAL — the task may be anything: code, research, architecture design, writing an essay, a 3D model, data analysis, UX, content, mixed. There is NO fixed task-type switch.
- The examples below (code / research / content / data …) are ILLUSTRATIVE, not an exhaustive list. YOU must derive what fits THIS task, using your judgement. Do not mechanically pick a template; reason about what "good" means here.

1. HOW TO BUILD THE PLAN (method, not just shape):
- Start from the END GOAL and the real consumer/reader, not from a fixed structure. Derive: what does an EXCELLENT result look like, and what DEPTH is required.
- From the goal, derive the goal's FACETS (the distinct things the result must deliver — e.g. correctness, understandability, coherent narrative, navigation, a working artifact). Every facet must be covered by at least one plan item (see 12, traceability).
- Only THEN decompose into steps. The plan must LEAD TO THE GOAL, not to "the mechanical checks pass".
- Carry a short ARGUMENT in the plan: one paragraph on WHY this structure reaches the goal.
- If you lack enough understanding to plan well, DO NOT decompose blindly — first do analysis: run a child flow (moira/todo-list autonomous research, moira/quick-task, or a child moira/robust-task for a large sub-topic) or an explicit analysis step, THEN plan.

2. STEP GRANULARITY (your lever on review overhead):
- Each step = one logical unit of work (not too small, not too large).
- Each step gets ONE gate review. So STEP SIZE IS YOUR LEVER on the number of reviews: if you have many small same-type actions, fold them into ONE bigger step with one gate — do not shatter them into 40 micro-steps.
- A big/multi-step item may DELEGATE its execution to a child flow (moira/quick-task with review, moira/todo-list autonomous, or a child moira/robust-task) via start({ parentExecutionId }). Two recipes: (a) "plan-flow → execution sub-flows" — this flow builds the plan, items launch child flows to execute; (b) "main work → nuance sub-flow" — do the core, then a child task finishes all the nuances.
- Avoid micro-steps ("create file") and mega-steps ("implement feature").

3. VERIFIABILITY BY THE APPROPRIATE METHOD (do NOT ban quality):
- Every step must be verifiable, but BY THE METHOD THAT FITS IT: factual / code / build / links → verify with TOOLS (run it, read the real code, check the reference). Quality / clarity / depth / narrative coherence / fitness-for-reader → verify by READING against an explicit rubric and judgement.
- "Avoid VAGUE criteria" (e.g. bare "works well") — YES. "Avoid QUALITATIVE criteria" — NO. For research/writing/design, quality IS the criterion; you are REQUIRED to state HOW it will be judged (the rubric), not forbidden from it.
- YOU MUST formulate the fitting verification approach for THIS task, whatever it is. (Illustrative rubrics: code → build/tests/lint pass, no hallucinated paths; research → read as a novice (every term introduced before use) + expert (real depth: math derived not shown as code; real mechanism, not a name-drop) + editor (coherent narrative, not fragments); content → reader-walkthrough (1 click to definition+example), narrative, no meta-marks; data → conclusion backed by the real data, alternatives considered.)

4. COMPLETENESS & DEPTH:
- All user requirements AND all goal facets must be covered by steps. No implicit assumptions.
- DEPTH over breadth: state the required depth per topic (better 6 well-explained than 10 shallow). Each step says what artifacts it produces AND to what depth.

5. SELF-SUFFICIENCY:
- Each step contains ALL information needed for execution: why, what to do, which files to read/modify, where to save, what to commit, and ITS OWN GATE (see 10).
- No references to "previous steps"; full file paths, not relative references.

6. RESILIENCE:
- Plan must work even if the agent loses context between steps (session archival). Each step executable in isolation from its own description.

7. STRUCTURED REASONING:
- Chain-of-thought for complex steps; explicitly define methods and output formats; document reasoning for non-obvious decisions.

8. SUCCESS CRITERIA & HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP:
- Success criteria defined BEFORE work starts, covering the goal (incl. the utility/depth axis where relevant), not only correctness. Plan shown to the user before execution; escalation available.

9. ATOMICITY & CONDITIONAL REDUNDANCY (no "global scope", but no ritual bloat):
- An agent often receives ONE plan item in isolation — other items and top-level "general rules" are NOT in its context.
- So each item restates the nuances it needs, the relevant original requirements, and the goal/quality anchor for the item.
- DUPLICATE a cross-cutting action into every item ONLY when it genuinely applies (e.g. "append a progress report", "run the tests", "make a commit"). Do NOT duplicate mechanical boilerplate into an item just to satisfy a rule when it adds nothing for that item — redundancy serves the item's isolation and the goal, it is not a checkbox. Judge per item.

10. ITEM STRUCTURE (template for each plan item — now includes the item's GATE):
N. **Task name** (what we're doing)
   Why: (problem + the original requirement / goal facet it serves)
   What to do:
   - specific action 1 with full file paths
   - specific action 2, save to /full/path
   - the cross-cutting actions that genuinely apply
   Serves goal facet: (which facet(s) from step 1 — for traceability)
   Expected output: (specific)
   Execution: DELEGATE (this item needs an autonomous intellectual pass over fresh full/large context — reasoning, judgment, deep reading; it MUST be run by a subagent given goal+context+freedom) OR INLINE (small, mechanical, low-context — the main agent may do it). In doubt on a research/reasoning item -> DELEGATE; the point of a subagent is autonomous intellectual work.
   GATE (acceptance for THIS item — YOU formulate it under the task):
   - technical floor (if any machine-checkable part exists — build/tests/links/paths — it MUST be here, as necessary-but-NOT-sufficient), AND
   - quality/substance criterion judged by the appropriate method (reading against a rubric for qualitative work).

11. NO TAIL DEGRADATION:
- The last items carry the SAME detail and quality as the first. Context volume is never an excuse to cut the tail.

12. GOAL TRACEABILITY (both directions):
- FORWARD: every item states which goal facet it serves (an item serving no facet is "work for the sake of a checkbox" — cut or re-aim it).
- BACKWARD: every goal facet is served by at least one item. A facet with NO item is a GAP surfaced at planning time (this is exactly how "narrative"/"navigation" silently fell through before).

13. PLAN IS NOT STRUCTURE-LOCKED (outcome-anchored):
- Anchor items on the RESULT/question, not on a pre-carved artifact ("understand what X teaches us", not "produce page 51"). The right structure often only emerges during execution.
- Mark genuinely provisional structural items as PROVISIONAL — their revision mid-execution is NORMAL, not an emergency and not "unfinished". (Provisional ≠ an excuse to under-deliver; do not silently narrow scope — see the revise directives.)

14. RESEARCH CORPUS & READING DISCIPLINE (non-dodgeable — this is a research flow):
- Planning, per-step execution, and every gate review are performed by SUBAGENTS (teammates), not ad-hoc by the main agent — each is a PEER with full judgment, handed goal + context + freedom (see the peer principle in every subagent brief), never caged.
- Every subagent MUST first read the WHOLE research corpus in full — every file listed in the corpus manifest (corpus-manifest.md), top to bottom — BEFORE doing anything else. A partial/selective read = the work is NOT done. WHY (the peer rationale): the parts are entangled — a conclusion here rests on reasoning elsewhere, through links that are conceptual and NOT findable by grep — so only a full read, holding the whole in your head, lets you judge whether it is sound. There is NO ledger and NO proof-of-read to fill in: the guarantee is that a skim cannot fake a real senior judgment, and a peer who also read everything will notice if it was faked.
- grep / ripgrep / search / find-in-files / selective / head / tail / line-range reads are fine as a NAVIGATION aid or a mechanical fact-check (does a link resolve, does a build/test pass), but NEVER a substitute for reading and NEVER how you judge soundness/quality.
- The corpus is FROZEN-BUT-EXPANDABLE: row 1 is always task-requirements.md (the frozen goal); any subagent that finds a new in-scope source APPENDS it to the manifest (path + line count + reason) and reads it. Growing the corpus is normal; silently NARROWING scope is forbidden.

[BUILD THE PLAN FOR INTELLIGENT AUTONOMOUS AGENTS, NOT A MACHINE]
Where an item is intellectual work, frame it as a GOAL + the CRITERIA for a good result and TRUST the executing agent (a peer with full judgment) to decide HOW. Do NOT pre-script every micro-move, do NOT shatter reasoning into mechanical coordinate-steps, do NOT cage the executor. An item may be "conduct an autonomous intellectual pass: <goal>, judged by <criteria>" rather than a scripted sequence. Mechanical granularity is right ONLY for genuinely mechanical work.

[JUDGMENT IS NOT A COORDINATE / CONDITIONAL FLOOR]
The technical floor exists ONLY where a genuinely machine-checkable part exists; many research/reasoning items have NONE — do not invent one, do not anchor to lines, do not build a coverage grid. For judgment claims the acceptance is a reasoned assessment, not coordinates.

[OUTPUT QUALITY RUBRIC] (the substance bar for every deliverable where the task is research/writing/explanatory):
 - EXPLANATORY PROSE, not a telegraphic term-stream: connected narrative with intro and conclusion; code/data woven into the flow, not dumped as labelled blocks.
 - Every mechanism/term gives WHAT (plain-words essence before first use) -> WHY (the problem it solves; what a naive approach would do) -> HOW (enough for the reader to get the idea), and ONLY THEN a reference as deepening — never a bare "see X.Y" IN PLACE of understanding.
 - CROSS-LINK every reference to its definition+example where the medium allows.
 - NO process meta-marks in the deliverable ("review done", "for engineer", "step N trace").
 - REWRITE telegraphic passages into explanatory ones — do NOT merely gloss/annotate on top.
 - Real DEPTH over breadth; no name-drop passing as coverage.

[PLAN-ITEM INVARIANTS] (the planner WRITES these into every plan item; the gate re-checks them): read the whole corpus first; produce explanatory narrative not tags; give WHAT/WHY/HOW per mechanism; cross-link every reference; no process meta-marks; hit the required depth; and restate the specific goal/requirements the item serves (so an isolated executor keeps them). Violating ANY invariant fails the item even if everything else is perfect.

[REVIEWER CALIBRATION] (every gate reviewer): calibrated to FIND defects, not to confirm a pass. Default stance: suspicion. A GREEN verdict is the EXCEPTION, earned only after a full end-to-end read as a stumbling novice found nothing wrong. Do not wave things through or grade on "most of it is fine". issues=0 ONLY if, reading as the target reader, you stumble NOWHERE.

R-0 (FINDING = CLASS): any defect found is a CLASS — fix/flag every instance of that pattern across the whole artifact or plan, not just the one spot.
R-1 (QUALITY BY READING): quality/clarity/depth/coherence is judged by READING against the rubric; scripts/grep/counting are allowed ONLY for a pure technical floor (build, tests, links, paths) — never as a proxy for quality.

15. OUTCOME-DEPENDENT / CASCADING WORK (do NOT over-plan) — extends §13 (outcome-anchored / PROVISIONAL):
- Some work is OUTCOME-DEPENDENT: a later step depends on the RESULT of an earlier one. Example:
  refactoring or extending a reasoned chain (aspect -> conclusion -> next investigation built on it
  -> next conclusion, many times). If the user asks to fix or open up an EARLY link, that can cascade
  into rethinking and rewriting everything downstream. The shape of step N genuinely depends on the
  actual result of step N-1 — which does not exist yet.
- Therefore you CANNOT fully plan such work upfront, and you MUST NOT fake a detailed downstream plan
  (that is false precision — it will be wrong the moment the first result comes in). Do not try to
  pre-plan the fix of an early conclusion AND how every later conclusion will change; you don't have
  the information yet, and pretending you do is the mistake.
- Instead: plan the NEAR HORIZON concretely, mark the rest PROVISIONAL, and encode the re-planning
  point EXPLICITLY. Choose the approach that fits (your judgment):
  A. CHILD-FLOW DECOMPOSITION WITH INHERITED CONTEXT. Make each dependent chunk a CHILD flow launched
     with start({ parentExecutionId: <this execution> }). CRITICAL: the child must INHERIT this flow's
     context — hand it the overall GOAL, the frozen task-requirements.md, the corpus-manifest, the
     specific sub-goal, AND the relevant RESULTS of the prior stages. A child run in isolation, with
     only its narrow slice, will drift from the whole — that is exactly what must not happen. When the
     child returns, RE-ASSESS against the real result and only THEN plan the next chunk.
  B. PLANNED RECURSIVE REPLAN. Put an EXPLICIT plan item whose job is: "using the results of the
     previous stage(s), DECIDE how to expand/reshape the remaining plan", and route it through
     teleport-replan. That replan may itself uncover further coupled changes that need ANOTHER explicit
     replan — recursion here is NORMAL and expected, not a failure or a stuck loop. The plan openly
     contains decision/replan items instead of pretending to know the downstream shape.
- WHEN this is the better approach (examples — recognize the shape, don't force a full plan):
   · Refactoring/deepening a research report whose reasoned chain has an EARLY conclusion you're asked
     to fix ("engine X doesn't fit our needs"): fixing it can invalidate every later conclusion built
     on it — you can't plan the downstream rewrite until you see how the early fix actually lands.
   · An R&D investigation where each finding determines the NEXT question — you cannot know step 5's
     topic until steps 1–4's results are in.
   · An architecture-design task where evaluating one alternative reveals a constraint that reshapes
     WHICH alternatives are even viable.
   · A source/dependency exploration where reading one source surfaces new must-read sources that
     change the scope.
- RESEARCH DEFAULT: for research / R&D projects this outcome-dependent style (near horizon concrete,
  tail PROVISIONAL, replan from the ACTUAL results) is OFTEN the RIGHT DEFAULT — genuinely
  fully-upfront-plannable research is the EXCEPTION, not the rule. Prefer it whenever the work is
  investigative and later steps hinge on what earlier steps find.
- MID-EXECUTION REPLAN IS ALWAYS ALLOWED (not only for cascades): replan the moment you realize,
  during the work, that you MISSED something, received NEW INPUTS, or a NEW ASPECT of the task
  surfaced. Realizing the current plan no longer fits the real task is a NORMAL, expected trigger for
  teleport-replan — never a failure and never a stuck loop.
- Either way: don't silently narrow scope, keep the frozen requirements/goal, and let the actual
  results — not a guessed upfront structure — drive the tail.
